Children's & juvenile life insurance: a child policy or a child rider?

Children's life insurance, also called juvenile life insurance, is usually a small whole life policy that a parent or grandparent buys on a child or grandchild. The child can keep it as an adult. It is not for everyone. Here is what it does, and how it compares with a child rider on a parent's policy. We price both side by side.

Reviewed by Luay Sadqi, Licensed Agent · NPN 21370662 · Updated November 2026

Schedule an appointment Call (301) 615-8289

What a child's policy does

  • Locks in insurability. As long as premiums are paid, the coverage stays in force even if health conditions appear later. Many policies include the right to buy more coverage at set ages without health questions.
  • Usually level premiums. The premium is set by the child's age at purchase. On many policies it stays level, but terms vary, so check the policy.
  • Builds cash value slowly. Whole life accumulates cash value the owner can borrow against. In the early years it is small.
  • Covers final costs. No parent wants to think about it, but the benefit would pay funeral costs and allow time away from work.

Video transcript
Two ways to cover a child with life insurance, side by side. The first way is usually a small whole life policy on the child. A parent or grandparent buys it. The child can keep it as an adult. It locks in insurability. Coverage stays in force while premiums are paid, even if health conditions appear later. It builds cash value slowly. The second way is a child rider on a parent's term policy. If you buy term life, you may be able to add one for all your children. It usually can be converted to the child's own policy later. A child policy is permanent. The child can keep it. A rider is often enough when the goal is simply protection during childhood. A child depends on your income far more than you depend on a policy on the child. So parents should have their own coverage in place first. A child's whole life policy is not a college savings plan. Its cash value grows slowly in the first decade. If saving for education is the goal, compare dedicated options too. Want to talk it through? Schedule a time at honorbrook-insurance.com or call (301) 615-8289.

The alternative: a child rider

If you are buying term life for yourself, most carriers let you add a child rider that covers all your children for a small added premium. It usually can be converted to the child's own permanent policy later. For families whose goal is simply protection during childhood, a rider is often enough.

A note on college savings: A child's whole life policy is life insurance. It is not a college savings plan, and its cash value grows slowly in the first decade. If saving for education is the goal, compare dedicated options too. See life insurance vs. a 529 plan.

Who usually buys one

  • Families with a history of health conditions that could make coverage hard to get later
  • Grandparents who want to give something that lasts
  • Parents who want a small permanent policy in place before the child is grown

Parents should have their own coverage in place first. A child depends on your income far more than you depend on a policy on the child.

Common questions

Children's Life Insurance FAQ

Is children's life insurance worth it?
It is worth considering when you want to lock in a child's insurability or give a permanent policy. If you only want protection while the child is young, a child rider on a parent's term policy may be enough. We price both side by side.
Who can buy a policy on a child?
A parent, grandparent, or legal guardian can usually apply. Carriers set their own rules on who may own the policy and how much coverage is allowed.
What is a guaranteed insurability rider?
It gives the insured the right to buy more coverage at set ages or life events without answering health questions.
Can the child take over the policy later?
Often, yes. Ownership can usually be transferred to the child as an adult. The premium usually stays level after the transfer, but check the policy's terms.

One honest call can make all the difference.
